name: Generalized anxiety disorder
dsmPointer: See DSM-5-TR: Anxiety Disorders — Generalized Anxiety Disorder
summary: Chronic worry that moves from topic to topic, runs ahead of the real risk and resists the client's efforts to set it aside. Worry often feels like a way to stay prepared or avoid being caught off guard, yet it rarely ends in a decision, and intolerance of uncertainty shows up as reassurance seeking, over-planning or putting decisions off. Over months the body carries the load as tension and poor rest. Some clients describe mainly physical complaints. It often co-occurs with depression and other anxiety conditions. For clinician review only; this is not a diagnosis.

durationGate.note: Ask how long worry has filled ordinary days and whether there have been worry-free stretches. ICD-11 describes a duration of at least several months. Confirm the timing requirement in DSM-5-TR.

ruleOuts.label: Hyperthyroidism
ruleOuts.note: Can cause restlessness, tremor, poor sleep and anxiety. Consider thyroid testing through the client's medical provider.

ruleOuts.label: Other medical conditions with anxiety as a direct effect
ruleOuts.note: For example cardiac arrhythmia, chronic lung disease, uncontrolled diabetes or neurological illness. Coordinate with medical care when onset is late in life or tied to a new illness.

ruleOuts.label: Delirium (sudden confusion)
ruleOuts.note: Confusion, drowsiness or attention that comes and goes over hours or days, often with an infection, surgery, dehydration, alcohol or sedative withdrawal or a medicine change, points to delirium (ICD-10-CM F05; ICD-11 6D70). It needs same-day medical assessment, not a mental health formulation (NICE CG103).

ruleOuts.label: Mild or major neurocognitive disorder
ruleOuts.note: A gradual decline in memory, thinking, planning or daily functioning, especially in later life, calls for a cognitive evaluation through primary care or a memory service (ICD-10-CM G31.84, F06.7x or F03.9x; ICD-11 6D71 or 6D80-6D8Z). Low mood, apathy, anxiety or new psychotic symptoms can be early signs (NICE NG97).

ruleOuts.label: Medication effects
ruleOuts.note: Corticosteroids, stimulants, bronchodilators, thyroid hormone and some other medicines can cause anxiety or insomnia. Review the medication list with the prescriber.

ruleOuts.label: Caffeine, stimulants or nicotine
ruleOuts.note: High intake can mimic or worsen chronic tension and poor sleep.

ruleOuts.label: Alcohol or sedative withdrawal
ruleOuts.note: Daily rebound anxiety between drinks or doses can look like generalized worry. Refer for medical assessment if withdrawal is possible. This app does not store substance-use information.

ruleOuts.label: Worry better explained by another mental health condition
ruleOuts.note: When worry keeps returning to one theme, that theme usually points to the better fit (see the differentials list). GAD worry is broad and shifts between topics.

specifiers.label: Predominantly somatic presentation (descriptive)
specifiers.note: Some clients report muscle pain, headaches, stomach upset or fatigue rather than 'worry'. Ask about the content of their thoughts and how much time they spend thinking about problems.

specifiers.label: Late-life onset (descriptive)
specifiers.note: New generalized anxiety after mid-life calls for a careful medical and medication review.

differentials.label: Illness anxiety disorder (ICD-10-CM title: Hypochondriasis)
differentials.distinguishing: One theme dominates: health. The client scans the body, researches symptoms and seeks medical reassurance that does not last.

differentials.label: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (ICD-10-CM title: Mixed obsessional thoughts and acts)
differentials.distinguishing: The thoughts feel alien to the client's values and are neutralized by rituals; GAD worry is about plausible everyday problems and feels like the client's own thinking.

differentials.label: Adjustment disorder with anxiety
differentials.distinguishing: The anxiety has a clear starting point in a recent life event and stays focused on it; expect it to settle as the client adapts or the situation resolves.

differentials.label: Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition (ICD-10-CM title: Anxiety disorder due to known physiological condition)
differentials.distinguishing: A medical illness, such as an overactive thyroid, is producing the anxiety through its effects on the body; symptoms rise and fall with that illness.

differentials.label: Social anxiety disorder (ICD-10-CM title: Social phobia, unspecified)
differentials.distinguishing: Worry centers on being judged or embarrassed by others.

differentials.label: Major depressive disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Repetitive thinking is mostly about past failures, guilt or worthlessness, alongside low mood or loss of interest. Both conditions often co-occur.

comorbidities.label: Major depressive disorder
comorbidities.note: GAD and depression co-occur often and share features such as poor sleep, fatigue and poor focus. Screen for both, and ask directly about suicidal thoughts.

comorbidities.label: Panic disorder
comorbidities.note: Some clients with chronic worry also have unexpected panic attacks. Assess panic separately.

comorbidities.label: Posttraumatic stress disorder
comorbidities.note: Worry that centers on safety after a traumatic event may reflect PTSD. Ask about trauma history.

comorbidities.label: Insomnia
comorbidities.note: Sleep problems are common and may need their own treatment, such as CBT for insomnia.

interventions.name: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for GAD
interventions.evidence: NICE CG113 (2011; 2020 surveillance kept the recommendations): individual high-intensity CBT is a recommended option at step 3 of stepped care. APA Division 12 lists CBT for GAD (check the current rating).
interventions.note: Targets worry processes, intolerance of uncertainty and avoidance. NICE describes weekly sessions over about 3 to 4 months.

interventions.name: Applied relaxation
interventions.evidence: NICE CG113 lists applied relaxation as an alternative high-intensity psychological intervention to CBT at step 3. A 2013 review (Hayes-Skelton et al.) describes it as one of the efficacious treatments for GAD.
interventions.note: Teaches clients to spot early signs of tension and relax quickly in daily situations. Progressive muscle relaxation is the first skill; the PMR home-practice handout supports this.

interventions.name: Progressive muscle relaxation home practice
interventions.evidence: Component of applied relaxation (NICE CG113). Relaxation training shows moderate effects on anxiety in a meta-analysis (Manzoni et al., 2008). NCCIH: relaxation techniques are generally safe for healthy people, though a few people report more anxiety.
interventions.note: Short daily practice with a tension log. Adjust for pain, injury, pregnancy or medical conditions. Warn clients that relaxing can briefly increase anxiety for some people.

interventions.name: Low-intensity options: guided self-help and psychoeducational groups
interventions.evidence: NICE CG113 step 2 options for GAD.
interventions.note: Suitable for milder presentations or while waiting for therapy. Review progress and step up if there is no improvement.

interventions.name: Worry time (worry postponement)
interventions.evidence: Common component of CBT protocols for GAD; limited evidence as a stand-alone technique.
interventions.note: The client sets aside a short daily time to worry and postpones worries until then. Pair it with a worry log.

interventions.name: Mindfulness-based approaches (complementary)
interventions.evidence: NCCIH notes evidence that mindfulness and meditation may help anxiety, including a 2023 randomized trial in which MBSR was noninferior to escitalopram.
interventions.note: Offer as an adjunct or alternative based on client preference. Adapt for trauma history (e.g., eyes-open options).

interventions.name: Referral for medication evaluation
interventions.evidence: NICE CG113 names an SSRI (sertraline) as the first-line medication for GAD at step 3.
interventions.note: Refer to psychiatry, a primary care provider or a psychiatric nurse practitioner. Prescribing decisions rest with the prescriber.

culturalNotes: In many settings, chronic worry is described through idioms like 'thinking too much', 'nerves' or 'nervios'. These overlap only in part with GAD, depression or PTSD; ask what the phrase means for the client rather than treating it as a symptom label.

Clients from cultures that discourage talking about emotions may present with headaches, stomach upset, fatigue or body pain. Ask about worry content and daily functioning, and coordinate with medical care.

Some worry is a realistic response to poverty, discrimination, immigration stress or unsafe housing. Separate realistic concerns, which may need practical help or referral, from worry that is out of proportion.
GAD-7 has been studied in many countries and languages, but cut-offs and item performance can differ across groups. Use validated translations and interpret scores alongside the interview.
Use a trained professional interpreter, not family members, for assessment in a language other than English.

If a client draws on prayer, scripture, meditation or other spiritual practices to manage worry, explore this respectfully. Use spiritual or faith-integrated approaches only when the client asks for them and after informed consent (see the AACC Code of Ethics for faith-based counselors).

redFlagRules.message: Manic or hypomanic signs are documented in this input. Screen for bipolar disorder (ICD-10-CM F31.x) and refer for psychiatric evaluation before treatment planning.
Psychotic symptoms are documented in this input and are not part of this pattern. Consider a psychotic disorder, substance effects or a medical cause, and refer for an urgent psychiatric evaluation.
Possible acute confusion is documented. Delirium and other medical causes can mimic this pattern; arrange a same-day medical assessment before relying on this suggestion.
